title: Compare farm designs, rates and build costs
summary: Choose a design for your edition, available materials and target output, then measure what reaches storage.

body.text: Start with a survival goal you can measure. If you need 12 stacks of cane for a trading session, your target is 768 cane. That gives you a way to judge whether a compact build is already large enough.
Read a farm rate in context

McFarms lists a TheySix Java flying-machine build for cane and bamboo at over 100,000 items per hour. The edition, the items counted and the design all matter. You cannot use that figure to predict the sugar cane collected by one module of Bedrock B172.

head: Record for each design
Why it changes the choice
rows: A Java design and a Bedrock design can harvest the same crop with different mechanisms. Match the tutorial to the revision of the world or schematic.
Output unit and number of modules
A combined bamboo-and-cane total does not tell you the cane yield. A whole installation and a single row need separate measurements.
Count the costly components first. Then include the collection line, storage, clearance for moving parts and access for repairs.
A high rate may depend on a steady bone meal supply or on the player keeping every module active. Record the conditions you can reproduce.

body.text: Time a run in the world download

items: Use the edition and version you intend to play. Let the farm reach its usual operating state, clear the output chest, and note the active module count.
Stay at the chosen operating position. Time several complete harvests and count only the target item delivered to storage.
Multiply the collected count by 60 and divide by the minutes elapsed. For example, 480 cane in 20 minutes gives 1,440 per hour. At that pace, 768 cane takes about 32 minutes.
Repeat the run. If drops pile up before storage, clear that bottleneck and measure again before spending materials on another module.

body.text: When two designs meet your target in the time available, compare the materials you still need to gather and the space you can spare. Keep the creator and revision with your notes so you can find the same design when a game update changes its behavior.
References: McFarms’ TheySix sugar cane and bamboo listing, Farmly’s material-list guide, and TMC Catalogue’s complete Java systems and revision guidance.
